name: Gabriel to Mary and the leap in Elizabeth's womb
scope: The two annunciation scenes that open Luke, told as one paired story. T1: in a house in Nazareth the angel Gabriel appears to a young woman named Mary and greets her -- 'Hail, thou that art highly favoured' (Luke 1:28) -- and tells her she will bear a son and call him Jesus. T2: Mary's astonished question, 'How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?' (Luke 1:34) and Gabriel's sign -- her older cousin Elizabeth, thought barren, is already six months pregnant. T3: Mary hurries into the hill country to a town of Judah, and when she greets Elizabeth the baby inside Elizabeth LEAPS in her womb -- the future John the Baptist, jumping at the voice of the mother of Jesus (Luke 1:41). T4: Mary's song in reply, called the Magnificat -- 'My soul doth magnify the Lord ... he hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree' (Luke 1:46-52) -- a poem sung in monasteries every evening for 1,500 years. T4b: the parallel scene the bank should key too -- Gabriel had already come, months earlier, to Elizabeth's husband Zacharias in the Temple at the hour of incense, and struck him DUMB for doubting the promise; he only spoke again when he wrote 'His name is John' on a tablet (Luke 1:8-22, 1:63). T5: Gabriel's title, 'the angel of the annunciation', becomes the name for the whole scene; the moment Mary says 'be it unto me according to thy word' (Luke 1:38) is what Christian art has painted, on walls and altarpieces, more times than any other single sentence in the Bible. Further rungs: the LILY in Mary's hand as the standard painterly signal (from Fra Angelico onward, not in the text); the traditional feast dates -- Annunciation on 25 March, exactly nine months before Christmas.
source: PRIMARY: Gospel of Luke 1:5-56 (Annunciation to Zacharias, Annunciation to Mary, Visitation, Magnificat, birth-and-naming of John). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Annunciation' and 'Visitation (Christianity)' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- the Gabriel scenes in Luke, the traditional 25 March feast, the Magnificat as one of the three Lucan canticles, Fra Angelico's Annunciation at San Marco; Grokipedia 'Magnificat' for the liturgical usage. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV wording of each cited verse before quoting.
framing_note: SCENE-LED story ladder that pairs the two Lucan annunciations. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (a baby jumping in the womb at another woman's greeting) and T4b (a priest struck mute in the Temple and writing the child's name on a tablet). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: the stem describes the scene -- the angel in the doorway, the hill-country greeting, the tablet -- and the answer is the NAMED THING (Gabriel, the Magnificat, John). Never let the stem call the angel Gabriel and then ask his name. SYMMETRIC-VOICE check: told as story-of-Mary-and-Elizabeth, the same neutral narrative voice used for Frigg mourning Balder or Deirdre foreseeing sorrow -- no 'the Lord's mother', no 'our Blessed Mother', no 'the fulfilment of Isaiah 7:14'. Just Mary, Elizabeth, Gabriel, the tablet, the song. DISTRACTOR MINE: the other named biblical angels (Michael, Raphael, Uriel), the other Marys (Magdalene, of Bethany, of Clopas), other biblical songs (Hannah's, Zechariah's Benedictus, Simeon's Nunc Dimittis), and other 'barren woman conceives' scenes (Sarah, Hannah, Rachel).
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Nazareth and Ein Karem as PLACES -- theology owns what HAPPENED there in story. HISTORY owns Herod's political reign; here Gabriel is the story-frame, not politics.

name: Bethlehem: the manger and the shepherds
scope: The Nativity night as Luke tells it. T1: Mary and Joseph travel from Nazareth to Bethlehem because the emperor Augustus has ordered a census, and there is 'no room for them in the inn' (Luke 2:7). T2: Mary gives birth in a stable and lays the baby in a MANGER -- a feeding trough for animals -- wrapped in swaddling clothes. T3: out in the fields nearby, shepherds are 'keeping watch over their flock by night' (Luke 2:8) when an angel appears and 'the glory of the Lord shone round about them' -- and the shepherds are terrified. T4: the angel's announcement -- 'Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy ... unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour' (Luke 2:10-11) -- and the sign given is that they will find the baby 'wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger'. T4b: then 'a multitude of the heavenly host' bursts out singing 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men' (Luke 2:13-14). T5: the shepherds go running to Bethlehem and find the scene exactly as told; Luke adds that Mary 'kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart' (Luke 2:19). Further rungs: the ox and the donkey at the manger come from later tradition (drawn from Isaiah 1:3), not from Luke; Bethlehem's name is a Hebrew phrase meaning 'house of bread'; Francis of Assisi is credited with staging the first live nativity scene at Greccio, Italy, in 1223.
source: PRIMARY: Gospel of Luke 2:1-20 (KJV). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Nativity of Jesus' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- the Lucan sequence (census, no-room, manger, shepherds, angel chorus), the Isaiah 1:3 origin of the ox and ass in art, Bethlehem's name meaning, Francis at Greccio in 1223 as the first crib scene. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV verse wording before quoting; the Greek 'kataluma' vs 'pandocheion' point (Luke's 'inn' may be a guest room in a house, not a commercial hostel -- flag but do NOT seed as a rung, keep the traditional scene).
framing_note: The most universally-known Christian scene, taught story-first. Dinner-test payoff: T4b (a whole SKY suddenly full of singing angels, above shepherds who thought they were alone). ACCURACY RAIL: the ox and donkey belong to LATER tradition, not to Luke -- if a rung uses them, say 'in the pictures we all know' or 'in Christmas art', never 'in the gospel'. The 'three shepherds' number is likewise not in the text. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told exactly the way one would tell the birth of Cuchulainn among the herds at Emain Macha or Zeus hidden in the cave on Crete -- no 'the Christ child', no 'Our Lord', no capital-B 'Baby'; just 'the baby', 'the child', 'Jesus'. DISTRACTOR MINE: the other Lucan nativity elements (Zacharias, John's birth in the hill country), other 'shepherd sees an angel' scenes (the annunciation to Gideon in Judges), other 'wrapped in cloth' details (Moses in the ark of bulrushes). CHOICE PARITY: if the answer is 'a manger', distractors are other named vessels/objects from the story world (a cradle, a basket, a wineskin, a fleece).
history_overlap: HISTORY owns Augustus's census as an imperial administrative fact and the debate over its dating -- do NOT seed a rung on 'when did this really happen'. GEOGRAPHY owns Bethlehem as a place; theology owns what HAPPENED there.

name: The Magi, the star, Herod, and the flight to Egypt
scope: Matthew's Nativity, which runs in a wholly different key from Luke's. T1: wise men -- 'Magi from the east' -- arrive in Jerusalem asking 'Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east' (Matthew 2:2). T2: they open their treasures at the child's feet and present three gifts, each a different substance -- gold, frankincense (an incense resin), and myrrh (a burial spice) (Matthew 2:11). T3: the wise men had first gone to King HEROD in Jerusalem; Herod, terrified of a rival king, told them to come back and report where the child was, 'that I may come and worship him also' (Matthew 2:8) -- a lie. Warned in a dream, they went home 'another way'. T4: when Herod realises he has been tricked, he orders every boy under two years old in Bethlehem and its region to be killed -- the Massacre of the Innocents (Matthew 2:16); Christian tradition since the second century has kept a feast for them on 28 December. T4b: Joseph, warned by an angel in a dream, has already fled with Mary and the child by night into Egypt (Matthew 2:13-14) -- the Flight into Egypt, painted a thousand times as a woman on a donkey with a baby, led by a man on foot. T5: they stay in Egypt until Herod dies, then return -- but Herod's son Archelaus is ruling Judea, so they settle instead in a small northern town, Nazareth (Matthew 2:22-23). T5b: the traditional NAMES of the wise men -- Caspar, Melchior, and Balthasar -- do NOT appear in Matthew; the gospel does not even say there were three, only that they brought three gifts. The three names are a later tradition, first attested in a 6th-century mosaic at Ravenna and in a manuscript called the Excerpta Latina Barbari.
source: PRIMARY: Gospel of Matthew 2:1-23 (KJV). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Biblical Magi' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- 'Magi from the east', gold/frankincense/myrrh, the star, Herod's questioning of the chief priests about Bethlehem (via Micah 5:2), the dream-warning, the flight into Egypt, the Massacre of the Innocents, the return to Nazareth via Archelaus's rule; the names Caspar/Melchior/Balthasar as later tradition first attested in the Excerpta Latina Barbari and the Sant'Apollinare Nuovo mosaic (c. 565) at Ravenna. Grokipedia 'Massacre of the Innocents' -- 28 December feast day (Holy Innocents' Day). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV verse wording before quoting.
framing_note: The Matthean Nativity as its OWN ladder, sharply distinct from Luke's shepherds. Dinner-test payoff: T5b (there is no '3' and no 'Caspar/Melchior/Balthasar' in the actual gospel -- the beloved detail is a LATER tradition). ACCURACY RAIL: Matthew calls them Magi (μάγοι), not 'kings' -- the 'three kings' framing is entirely medieval; do not put it in a stem as gospel. Second rail: the Slaughter of the Innocents is a hard beat -- state it once, as story, without lingering visual detail; the WEIGHT is that Joseph and Mary escaped in the night, not the body count. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same voice one would use for Uranus swallowing his children or Loki bringing doom to Balder -- 'Herod ordered', not 'the wicked King Herod carried out'. DISTRACTOR MINE: the other named biblical Herods (Herod Antipas the tetrarch who killed John the Baptist, Herod Agrippa in Acts), other biblical dreams-that-warn (Joseph's coat-of-many-colours brother in Genesis, Pharaoh, Daniel), other named royal gifts (the Queen of Sheba's spices in 1 Kings). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: the stem describes the scene (a star in the east, foreign visitors, treasures opened at a child's feet) and asks what the third gift was, or what Herod ordered next.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns Herod the Great as a political figure and the archaeology of the Herodian kingdom -- keep this ladder inside the story. GEOGRAPHY owns Egypt as a place; here it is the destination of the night flight, one line.

name: The boy Jesus in the Temple at twelve
scope: The only scene the gospels give from Jesus's childhood after the Nativity. T1: when Jesus is TWELVE, his parents take him to Jerusalem for the Passover feast, as they do every year (Luke 2:41-42). T2: on the way home they travel a whole day before they notice he is not in the caravan -- they had thought he was 'in the company' with other kin -- and they turn back to search Jerusalem for three days (Luke 2:44-46). T3: they finally find him in the TEMPLE, sitting among the teachers, 'both hearing them, and asking them questions', and everyone who heard him was 'astonished at his understanding and answers' (Luke 2:46-47). T4: Mary, half-scolding him, says 'Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing' (Luke 2:48). T5: the boy's reply -- his FIRST recorded words in the gospels -- 'How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?' (Luke 2:49). Further rungs: Luke closes the scene by saying he 'went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject unto them' (Luke 2:51), and 'increased in wisdom and stature' (Luke 2:52) -- the one line the New Testament gives us about the years between twelve and thirty.
source: PRIMARY: Gospel of Luke 2:41-52 (KJV). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Finding in the Temple' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- the age of 12, the three-day search, the teachers in the Temple, the 'my Father's business' reply as the fifth Joyful Mystery of the Rosary in Catholic tradition, and its status as the only canonical episode from Jesus's boyhood. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV verse wording before quoting.
framing_note: A compact family ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (his parents travel a whole DAY before noticing their son is missing -- because kids travelled with the aunts and uncles). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem sets the scene (Passover crowd, missing boy, three-day search, found among teachers) and the answer is the AGE (twelve), the LOCATION (Temple), or Jesus's actual REPLY. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same domestic-panic voice one would give the boy Fionn burning his thumb at Finegas's fire -- no capital-F 'Father', no 'the divine child'; just 'his mother', 'the boy', 'his answer'. DISTRACTOR MINE: other 'child prodigy' biblical scenes (young Samuel hearing the voice in the night, young David chosen over his brothers, young Daniel refusing the king's food), and other Passover-in-Jerusalem scenes from Jesus's ministry. Do NOT seed apocryphal 'Infancy Gospel of Thomas' stories (clay birds, cursed playmates) -- they are not canonical and the bank stays with the gospel scene.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns the Second Temple as a physical structure and Jerusalem as a place; here the Temple is the setting where a boy sat and asked questions.

name: John the Baptist: locusts, honey, and the dove at the Jordan
scope: The wild prophet at the river, and the baptism scene that opens the ministry. T1: John lives in the WILDERNESS of Judea, wearing 'raiment of camel's hair, and a leathern girdle about his loins' (Matthew 3:4), preaching that people should repent. T2: what he eats out there -- 'his meat was LOCUSTS and wild HONEY' (Matthew 3:4). T3: crowds come out from Jerusalem to hear him and he dunks them in the river JORDAN as a sign that they are washing away their old lives -- which gives him his name, 'the Baptist' (from a Greek word meaning 'the dipper'). T4: John's warning to the Pharisees and Sadducees who come to be baptised -- 'O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?' (Matthew 3:7). T4b: he tells the crowd that one is coming after him whose SANDALS he is not worthy to unloose (Mark 1:7). T5: Jesus comes down from Galilee to be baptised by John. John hesitates -- 'I have need to be baptised of thee' -- but Jesus insists. When Jesus comes up out of the water, 'the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a DOVE, and lighting upon him' (Matthew 3:16), and a voice from heaven says 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased' (Matthew 3:17). Further rungs: John's father Zacharias and mother Elizabeth (the same Elizabeth from the Visitation); his end -- BEHEADED by Herod Antipas at the request of Herodias's daughter, who danced for the king and asked for John's head on a platter (Mark 6:17-28).
source: PRIMARY: Matthew 3:1-17, Mark 1:1-11, Luke 3:1-22, John 1:19-34, Mark 6:14-29 (KJV). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'John the Baptist' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- camel-hair garment and leather belt, diet of locusts and wild honey, ministry at the Jordan, 'generation of vipers', the sandal-strap saying, baptism of Jesus with dove and voice from heaven, imprisonment and execution by Herod Antipas at the request of Salome (Herodias's daughter -- note: Salome is named in Josephus, not in Mark). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV verse wording; the 'Salome' name comes from Josephus's Antiquities 18.5.4, NOT from the gospels -- if the daughter is named at all, say 'in the historian Josephus'.
framing_note: The bridge ladder from Nativity to public ministry. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (he ate LOCUSTS -- actual insects -- and WILD HONEY, out in the desert) and T5 (a dove and a voice from the sky). ACCURACY RAIL: the daughter who danced is NOT named 'Salome' in the gospels -- that name comes from Josephus; if used, attribute it. Second rail: the 'wild honey' probably means bee honey found in rock hollows, and the 'locusts' were the insect (the alternative 'carob pods' reading is a fringe medieval attempt to soften it -- keep the insect). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of the Fianna's outsider fosterlings living rough in the forest, or of a Greek oracle-figure in a cave -- 'the wild man at the river', not 'the holy forerunner'. DISTRACTOR MINE: other biblical wilderness figures (Elijah on Horeb, the Rechabites), other river-crossing scenes (Joshua at the Jordan, Naaman dipping seven times in the Jordan, Elisha and the axe head), and other 'voice from heaven' scenes (the Transfiguration, Saul on the road to Damascus). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem gives the wilderness scene, the animal-hair coat, the crowds; the answer is what he ATE, what he SAID, or what came DOWN LIKE A DOVE.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns Herod Antipas and Herodias as political figures and Machaerus as an archaeological site (the fortress where John was killed, per Josephus); here the beheading is one rung of story, no politics.

name: Forty days in the wilderness: the three temptations
scope: The desert testing that follows the baptism. T1: after his baptism Jesus goes out alone into the wilderness, and stays there FORTY DAYS AND FORTY NIGHTS, eating nothing (Matthew 4:1-2, Luke 4:1-2). T2: at the end, when he is starving, the devil comes and tempts him three times -- and Jesus answers each time by quoting the book of Deuteronomy. T3: the FIRST temptation -- 'If thou be the Son of God, command that these STONES be made bread' (Matthew 4:3); Jesus replies 'Man shall not live by bread alone' (Matthew 4:4, quoting Deuteronomy 8:3). T4: the SECOND temptation -- the devil takes him to the pinnacle of the TEMPLE in Jerusalem and dares him to jump, saying that the angels will catch him (Matthew 4:5-6); Jesus replies 'Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God' (Matthew 4:7). T5: the THIRD temptation -- the devil takes him up 'into an exceeding high mountain', shows him 'all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them', and offers them all if Jesus will bow down and worship him (Matthew 4:8-9). Jesus refuses -- 'Get thee hence, Satan' (Matthew 4:10) -- and 'the devil leaveth him, and, behold, angels came and ministered unto him' (Matthew 4:11). Further rungs: the FORTY-day figure is the same length as Moses on Sinai and Elijah's journey to Horeb; the season of LENT (six weeks minus Sundays before Easter) is timed to it and is the reason for Christian fasting traditions.
source: PRIMARY: Matthew 4:1-11, Mark 1:12-13, Luke 4:1-13 (KJV). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Temptation of Christ' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- the three temptations in Matthew/Luke (order differs: Matthew ends with the mountain, Luke ends with the Temple), the fasting duration, each reply as a quote from Deuteronomy (8:3, 6:16, 6:13), the Lenten fast as its liturgical extension. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV verse wording; note Luke's order differs from Matthew's -- if a rung asks for order, use Matthew's.
framing_note: A three-scene ladder with a natural T3/T4/T5 pattern (one temptation per rung). Dinner-test payoff: T4 (thrown off a rooftop for the angels to catch him) and T5 (all the kingdoms of the world offered at once, from a mountain). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same voice one would use for the temptations of the Buddha under the bo tree or of Aeneas in the underworld -- 'a duel of quotations in the desert', not 'the Adversary tempts Our Lord'. Use plain 'the devil' (as the KJV does) rather than doctrinal titles ('the Prince of Darkness', 'the Fallen One'). DISTRACTOR MINE: other biblical wilderness sequences (Israel's 40 years, Elijah's 40 days to Horeb, Moses's 40 days on Sinai), other 'showed him all the kingdoms' scenes (Moses on Nebo seeing the Promised Land), and other biblical dares to jump (Peter walking on the water). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem describes the scene (starving man in the desert, tempter, cliff-top view of the world); the answer is the OBJECT of the temptation (stones/bread, the Temple pinnacle, the kingdoms) or the exact quoted reply.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the historical Judean wilderness geography -- here the wilderness is a story setting.

name: Water into wine at the wedding in Cana
scope: The first miracle in John's gospel. T1: Jesus, his mother Mary, and his disciples are guests at a wedding in a village called CANA in Galilee (John 2:1-2). T2: partway through the feast the wine RUNS OUT, and Mary tells Jesus. He answers, 'Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come' (John 2:4) -- yet Mary turns to the servants and simply says 'Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it' (John 2:5). T3: there are SIX stone waterpots standing there, used for Jewish ritual washing, each holding two or three firkins (roughly 20-30 gallons apiece). Jesus tells the servants to fill them 'to the brim' with water (John 2:6-7). T4: he tells them to draw some out and take it to the master of the feast (the 'governor of the feast') to taste. He does not know where it has come from -- and it is WINE, and he calls the bridegroom over to compliment him: 'Every man at the beginning doth set forth good wine ... but thou hast kept the good wine until now' (John 2:10). T5: John calls this 'the beginning of miracles' -- Jesus's first public sign, done at a friend's WEDDING, not in a temple or on a mountain, and preserving the party of two ordinary young people whose names the gospel never even gives. Further rungs: the six stone jars specifically 'after the manner of the purifying of the Jews' -- for a hand-and-vessel washing rite; the total volume works out to something like 120-180 gallons of wine, a superabundant, absurd amount for a village party.
source: PRIMARY: Gospel of John 2:1-11 (KJV). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Marriage at Cana' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- Cana in Galilee, six stone jars for Jewish purification each holding two-to-three metretes (a firkin is roughly a metretes, ~35 litres), the exchange with Mary, the master-of-the-feast's compliment, John's designation as 'the first of his signs', the enormous quantity implied. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV wording of Mary's 'whatsoever he saith unto you, do it' and the master's line.
framing_note: The bank's first MIRACLE ladder, kept scene-first. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (six stone WATER pots and a total of well over a hundred gallons of party wine) and T4 (the master of the feast praises the BRIDEGROOM for keeping the best wine till last, having no idea who actually made it). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Jesus turned water into wine' and then ask what happened; describe the JARS, the empty cellar, the master's compliment, and let the recall be the number six, the setting (a wedding), or the exact praise quote. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same voice as Dionysus turning a stream into wine on Andros, or the Dagda's cauldron of plenty -- as a wonder-scene, not as a lesson-with-a-moral. Do not gloss the miracle theologically. DISTRACTOR MINE: other water-related miracles (Moses striking the rock, Elijah and the widow's oil, the loaves and fishes) and other wedding scenes in the parables (the wise/foolish virgins, the wedding feast of the king's son). Note: John 2 is FIRST in the sign-sequence of John's gospel; do not conflate with the synoptic order.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Cana as a place (Kafr Kanna and Khirbet Qana are the two candidate sites -- do NOT seed a rung on which is 'really' Cana; that is a specialist archaeology question).

name: The storm on the sea and walking on the water
scope: The two great Sea-of-Galilee miracles that always come as a pair in memory. T1: the SEA OF GALILEE is a lake surrounded by hills where sudden storms funnel down the ravines and hit the water without warning. T2 (STILLING THE STORM): Jesus and the disciples are in a boat crossing the lake when a great storm breaks; he is ASLEEP on a pillow in the stern (Mark 4:38). The disciples wake him in a panic -- 'Master, carest thou not that we perish?' T3: he stands up, speaks to the wind and the sea -- 'Peace, be still' (Mark 4:39) -- and 'the wind ceased, and there was a great calm', and the disciples say 'What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?' (Mark 4:41). T4 (WALKING ON THE WATER): on another crossing the disciples are alone in the boat at night, rowing against the wind, and Jesus comes toward them WALKING on the water; they think he is a ghost and cry out (Matthew 14:22-26, Mark 6:45-50). T4b: PETER calls out -- 'Lord, if it be thou, bid me come unto thee on the water' -- and Jesus says 'Come'. Peter climbs over the side and walks a few steps on the water toward Jesus (Matthew 14:28-29). T5: the moment Peter looks at the WIND, he becomes afraid and starts to SINK, and cries 'Lord, save me' -- Jesus stretches out his hand, catches him, and says 'O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?' (Matthew 14:30-31); as soon as they climb back in the boat, the wind stops. Further rungs: the storm scene is in Matthew 8, Mark 4 and Luke 8 (Mark keeps the 'pillow'); the walking-on-water is in Matthew 14, Mark 6 and John 6, but ONLY Matthew has Peter climbing out.
source: PRIMARY: Mark 4:35-41 and Matthew 8:23-27 (stilling the storm); Matthew 14:22-33, Mark 6:45-52, John 6:16-21 (walking on the water) -- KJV. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Calming the storm' and 'Jesus walking on water' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- Sea of Galilee's storm-prone microclimate, the pillow in the stern as Mark's unique detail, the 'Peace, be still' rebuke, Peter's water-walk being unique to Matthew, the 'ghost' cry, the wind ceasing when Jesus enters the boat. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV wording of 'Peace, be still' and 'O thou of little faith'.
framing_note: A twin-scene ladder that keeps two lake miracles side by side; the answer hierarchy sits on VIVID ACTIONS and NAMED PLACE. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (asleep on a PILLOW in the stern while the boat is nearly capsized) and T4b (Peter actually climbing out and taking a few steps before the wind spooks him). ACCURACY RAIL: only MATTHEW has Peter walking out -- Mark and John cut straight from Jesus stepping in the boat to the wind stopping; if a rung tests source, key Matthew. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same wonder-voice one would give Manannan mac Lir riding his horse over the waves, or Poseidon striking the sea with his trident -- a lake-god scene, not a theological proof-text. DISTRACTOR MINE: other biblical water-scenes (Moses parting the Red Sea, Elijah and Elisha crossing the Jordan on dry ground, Jonah in the belly of the fish), other 'sleeping through a crisis' scenes (Jonah in the hold of the ship during his OWN storm -- a natural distractor), and the other Sea-of-Galilee miracle (the great catch of fish -- keep that in the resurrection ladder). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: describe the SCENE (dark night, wind against them, a figure walking on the water) and the answer is Peter's exact request, the pillow, or the rebuke to the storm.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns the Sea of Galilee as a lake; here it is the setting for a story.

name: Five loaves and two fishes: feeding the five thousand
scope: The only miracle recorded in all four gospels. T1: a crowd of about FIVE THOUSAND men (plus women and children, in Matthew's count) has followed Jesus into a lonely, grassy place beside the Sea of Galilee, and it is getting late (Matthew 14:15-21). T2: the disciples want to send them all home to buy food. Jesus says, 'They need not depart; give ye them to eat' -- and Philip protests that two hundred pennyworth (denarii) of bread would not be enough for each to have a little (John 6:7). T3: Andrew brings forward a small BOY who has 'five barley loaves and two small fishes' (John 6:9) -- the whole picnic, the whole supply. T4: Jesus tells the crowd to sit down on the GRASS 'by companies' of fifties and hundreds (Mark 6:39-40); he takes the loaves, looks up to heaven, BLESSES and BREAKS them, and hands the pieces to the disciples to distribute. Everyone eats until they are full. T5: they gather up the leftover fragments and fill TWELVE BASKETS -- one for each disciple -- with what is left over (Mark 6:43). Further rungs: a SECOND feeding miracle appears just a few chapters later in Matthew and Mark, with FOUR thousand fed from SEVEN loaves, leaving SEVEN baskets (Matthew 15:32-38, Mark 8:1-9); the numbers matter enough that Jesus later quizzes the disciples on them -- 'when I brake the five loaves ... how many baskets? ... when the seven ... how many?' (Mark 8:19-20). Only in JOHN's gospel is the boy with the picnic named as the source.
source: PRIMARY: Matthew 14:13-21, Mark 6:30-44, Luke 9:10-17, John 6:1-14 (five thousand); Matthew 15:32-39, Mark 8:1-10 (four thousand); Mark 8:14-21 (Jesus recalls the numbers). KJV. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV verse wording.

Dinner-test payoff: T3 (a little BOY with his lunch is where the whole miracle starts, and only John's gospel bothers to mention him) and T5 (TWELVE baskets left over -- MORE food after than before). ACCURACY RAIL: there are TWO feeding miracles, not one -- 5,000/5/2/12 and 4,000/7/-/7 -- and the bank should NOT let them be conflated in an answer stem. The 'boy with the lunch' appears in JOHN only; if a rung tests source, key John. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell the Dagda's inexhaustible cauldron feeding an army, or the horn of plenty at a Greek feast -- 'a picnic that ran on and on', not 'the eucharistic prefiguration'. Do not gloss theologically. DISTRACTOR MINE: the numbers themselves (make sure 5/2/12 answers do not have 7/-/7 as distractor unless the point is disambiguation), other biblical feedings (Elijah and the widow's oil, Elisha and the twenty loaves in 2 Kings 4:42-44 -- a genuine precursor scene), manna in the wilderness. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: the scene is the grassy field, the crowd, the child's picnic; the answer is the number of loaves, of fish, of baskets, or of thousands.
