name: The paralytic through the roof, and blind Bartimaeus
scope: Two healing scenes that live in memory for their vivid physical detail. T1 (THE ROOF): Jesus is teaching in a house in Capernaum, and the crowd is packed so tight that no one can get in through the door (Mark 2:1-2). T2: four men are carrying a paralysed friend on a mat to be healed; unable to get through the crowd, they climb up to the ROOF, break a hole in it, and LOWER him down on his mat right into the middle of the room in front of Jesus (Mark 2:3-4). T3: Jesus, seeing 'their faith' (the FOUR carrying the ONE), says to the paralysed man 'Son, thy sins be forgiven thee' (Mark 2:5) -- which shocks the scribes -- and then, to prove the point, 'Arise, take up thy bed, and walk' (Mark 2:11); the man gets up, folds his mat, and walks out. T4 (BARTIMAEUS): as Jesus is leaving JERICHO, a blind BEGGAR named BARTIMAEUS (the gospel means 'son of Timaeus') is sitting by the roadside; hearing that Jesus of Nazareth is passing, he shouts 'Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me' (Mark 10:47). The crowd tells him to be quiet; he shouts louder. T5: Jesus stops the whole crowd, calls him over -- and Bartimaeus THROWS OFF his cloak (which for a beggar was probably everything he owned) and runs to Jesus (Mark 10:50). Jesus asks the question the gospel highlights -- 'What wilt thou that I should do unto thee?' -- and the man answers 'Lord, that I might receive my sight' (Mark 10:51). Further rungs: the third healing scene the bank should key -- the woman with 'an issue of blood twelve years' who touches the HEM of Jesus's robe in a crowd and is healed instantly; Jesus feels 'virtue' go out of him and asks 'Who touched me?' (Mark 5:25-34); she comes forward trembling and is told 'Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole' (Mark 5:34).
source: PRIMARY: Mark 2:1-12, Mark 10:46-52, Mark 5:25-34 and parallels (KJV). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Healing the paralytic at Capernaum' and 'Bartimaeus' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- roof-opening scene, four bearers, 'take up thy bed and walk'; Bartimaeus meaning 'son of Timaeus', Jericho setting, throwing off cloak, 'What wilt thou that I should do unto thee', the naming of a healed beggar being unusual in the gospels. Grokipedia 'Hemorrhaging woman' -- twelve years, touching the fringe/hem, 'virtue' going out. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV wording; the 'roof' in Mark is likely a mud-and-thatch or tiled Palestinian roof that a person could physically dig through.
framing_note: A twin-scene healing ladder with a bonus mini-scene (the woman with the hem). Dinner-test payoff: T2 (four men actually TEARING A HOLE in someone's ROOF to lower their friend through) and T5 (a blind beggar throwing off the only cloak he owned to run to Jesus). ACCURACY RAIL: the healed beggar is 'Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus' in Mark, which is redundant on purpose -- Bar-Timaeus MEANS son of Timaeus in Aramaic; state that once. Second rail: the woman-with-the-hem story is embedded INSIDE the story of Jairus's daughter in Mark 5 -- the bank puts Jairus's daughter in the next ladder (raisings), so keep the hem scene here as a mini-rung. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell Cuchulainn's healing hands or Asclepius's temple cures -- as memorable scenes with named recipients, not as doctrinal proofs. DISTRACTOR MINE: other healing miracles (ten lepers, the centurion's servant, blind man of Bethsaida, blind man of Siloam), other 'through a hole in the roof' images (Rahab lowering the spies through the window). Note: Matthew and Luke also have blind men at Jericho -- Matthew has TWO, Mark and Luke have ONE named/unnamed -- key MARK's version because Bartimaeus is a named beggar. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: scene = the roof, the ropes, the mat, the crowd, the roadside beggar shouting; answer = the number of bearers, the name Bartimaeus, the thrown-off cloak, or Jesus's exact question.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Capernaum and Jericho as places; here they are settings.

name: Come forth: raising Jairus's daughter and Lazarus
scope: The two raising-from-death scenes. T1 (JAIRUS'S DAUGHTER): JAIRUS, a ruler of the synagogue, falls at Jesus's feet begging him to come and heal his 12-year-old daughter, who is dying (Mark 5:22-23). On the way, servants meet them with the news -- 'thy daughter is dead; why troublest thou the Master any further?' (Mark 5:35). T2: Jesus tells Jairus 'Be not afraid, only believe' (Mark 5:36), takes only Peter, James and John with him, sends the mourners out of the house saying 'the damsel is not dead, but sleepeth' (Mark 5:39) -- and they LAUGH him to scorn. T3: he takes the dead girl's hand and speaks TWO WORDS in Aramaic -- 'Talitha cumi' -- which Mark then translates for his Greek readers as 'Damsel, I say unto thee, arise' (Mark 5:41). She gets up and walks, and Jesus tells them, oddly, to give her something to eat (Mark 5:43). T4 (LAZARUS): a man named LAZARUS, who lives in BETHANY with his sisters Martha and Mary, falls sick. His sisters send word to Jesus, but Jesus deliberately waits two more days before setting out (John 11:1-6); by the time he arrives, Lazarus has been in the tomb FOUR days. T4b: Martha meets Jesus on the road -- 'if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died' -- and later, seeing Mary and the mourners weeping at the tomb, Jesus HIMSELF weeps: 'JESUS WEPT' (John 11:35), the shortest verse in the English Bible. T5: they come to the tomb, a cave with a stone across it. Jesus tells them to 'take ye away the stone'; Martha protests that Lazarus 'stinketh' after four days. Then Jesus cries with a loud voice, 'LAZARUS, COME FORTH' (John 11:43), and Lazarus walks out of the tomb, still wound up in the grave-clothes, his face bound in a napkin. Jesus says, 'Loose him, and let him go' (John 11:44). Further rungs: a third raising -- the son of the widow at NAIN, whom Jesus meets as a funeral procession is coming out of a village gate (Luke 7:11-15); Jesus stops the bier, says 'Young man, I say unto thee, Arise', and the dead son sits up.
source: PRIMARY: Mark 5:21-43 (Jairus's daughter, with the hemorrhaging woman inserted), Luke 7:11-17 (widow of Nain), John 11:1-44 (Lazarus). KJV. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Raising of Jairus's daughter' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- 'talitha cumi' as Aramaic preserved in Mark, translated for Greek audience, the two-word command, the taking-only-three disciples, telling them to give her food. Grokipedia 'Raising of Lazarus' -- Bethany, four days in the tomb, the sisters Martha and Mary (same Mary of Bethany who anoints Jesus's feet with spikenard), Jesus wept as John 11:35, 'Lazarus, come forth', bound in grave-clothes with the napkin. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV wording; 'talitha cumi' vowel-pointing (talitha koum/koumi) -- KJV has 'talitha cumi'.
framing_note: A paired-raising ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (Jesus preserves the actual Aramaic words 'Talitha cumi' -- a phrase kids can repeat out loud) and T4b (the shortest verse in the English Bible is 'Jesus wept'). ACCURACY RAIL: the sisters at Bethany are Martha and Mary of Bethany -- do NOT confuse this Mary with Mary Magdalene or with Mary the mother of Jesus. Second rail: 'Jesus wept' is famously the shortest verse in ENGLISH (KJV); in Greek it is not the shortest -- state it as an English-Bible fact. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told as one would tell Orpheus turning to look at Eurydice, or Balder's failed return -- as scenes of ordinary grief interrupted, not as doctrinal proofs of divinity. DISTRACTOR MINE: the other Marys (Magdalene, mother of Jesus, of Clopas), the other Lazarus (Lazarus and Dives in the parable -- keep that in the parables ladder), other raisings (Elijah with the widow of Zarephath's son, Elisha with the Shunammite's son, Peter raising Tabitha/Dorcas in Acts 9). Note: the widow-of-Nain rung should only appear if depth allows -- do NOT dilute the two named scenes. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: scene = a dying child, a shut tomb, weeping sisters; answer = the exact Aramaic phrase, Lazarus's four days, the shortest-verse fact.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Bethany as a place (modern al-Eizariya, named for Lazarus); here it is the setting.

name: The Good Samaritan on the Jericho road
scope: The most famous parable in Western culture, told as scene. T1: a lawyer stands up to test Jesus, asking 'And who is my neighbour?' (Luke 10:29). Jesus answers with a story. T2: 'A certain man went down from JERUSALEM to JERICHO, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead' (Luke 10:30). T3: the FIRST TWO who pass by are the respectable religious professionals of the day -- a PRIEST, who 'passed by on the other side'; then a LEVITE, who 'looked on him, and passed by on the other side' (Luke 10:31-32). T4: the THIRD traveller is a SAMARITAN -- a member of a group the lawyer's audience despised and considered heretical, whom no one would have expected to help a Jewish stranger. He stops. He 'had compassion on him', 'went to him', and 'bound up his wounds, pouring in OIL and WINE' (Luke 10:33-34). T4b: he lifts the wounded man onto his OWN BEAST, carries him to an inn, and takes care of him overnight. T5: leaving in the morning, the Samaritan hands the innkeeper TWO PENCE (two denarii, roughly two days' wages) and says 'take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee' (Luke 10:35) -- an OPEN account. Jesus then asks the lawyer, 'Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves?' and the lawyer, unable to bring himself to say the word 'Samaritan', says 'He that shewed mercy on him' -- and Jesus says 'Go, and do thou likewise' (Luke 10:36-37). Further rungs: the Jericho road drops about 3,300 feet in some 17 miles through desert wadis, notorious for bandits, and known in Jesus's time as 'the Bloody Way'.
source: PRIMARY: Gospel of Luke 10:25-37 (KJV). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Parable of the Good Samaritan' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- priest and Levite passing by, Samaritan stopping, oil and wine on the wounds, two denarii paid to the innkeeper with promise of more, the lawyer's inability to say 'Samaritan', the Jericho road's geography and 3,300-foot descent. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV wording for 'passed by on the other side' and the exact two-pence figure.
framing_note: PARABLE ladder that keeps the SCENE and the NAMED DETAILS (oil, wine, beast, two pence, priest, Levite, Samaritan). Dinner-test payoff: T4 (a hated foreigner is the HERO of the story a Jewish teacher tells to a Jewish lawyer) and T5 (an OPEN account at the inn -- 'whatever more you spend, I'll pay when I get back'). ACCURACY RAIL: this is a PARABLE, a made-up story Jesus tells -- do not present it as a historical event. The Samaritan-Jewish antagonism was real (Josephus records the Samaritans scattering bones in the Temple around 8 CE); if the tension is referenced, key that historicity to Josephus. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told as the SCENE, not the moral -- the DIRECTIVE 'love thy neighbour' is Leviticus 19:18, quoted by the lawyer, not Jesus's coinage; do not present the parable as inventing that command. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Lucan parables (Prodigal Son, Lost Sheep, Lazarus and Dives), other 'traveller in trouble' scenes (the Levite in Judges 19, Jonah), other 'oil and wine' pairs (Melchizedek's bread and wine, the ten virgins' oil). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: describe the ROAD, the beaten man, the two respectable passers-by; answer = the third traveller's ethnicity, the substances poured on the wound, the amount paid.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns the Jerusalem-Jericho road and its descent; keep that as one atmosphere-line, not a geology rung.

name: The Prodigal Son: the ring, the sandals, and the fatted calf
scope: The parable Rembrandt painted at the end of his life. T1: 'A certain man had two sons' (Luke 15:11). The YOUNGER son asks his father for 'the portion of goods that falleth to me' -- his share of the inheritance, in advance, while his father is still alive (Luke 15:12). The father gives it. T2: the younger son 'wasted his substance with riotous living' in 'a far country'; when a famine hits, he is broke, and takes the lowest job available -- feeding SWINE (to a Jewish audience, an unclean animal) -- and grows so hungry he 'would fain have filled his belly with the HUSKS that the swine did eat' (Luke 15:16). T3: 'when he came to himself' he says 'I will arise and go to my father' and rehearses the speech: 'Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, and am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants' (Luke 15:17-19). T4: while the son is 'yet a great way off', the father SEES him coming, and RUNS to meet him -- an old man running was undignified in Jesus's world -- and kisses him. Before the son can finish his prepared speech, the father is already shouting orders at the servants: 'Bring forth the BEST ROBE, and put it on him; and put a RING on his hand, and SHOES on his feet: and bring hither the FATTED CALF, and kill it; and let us eat, and be merry' (Luke 15:22-23). T5: the OLDER brother, coming in from working in the fields, hears the music and dancing, refuses to come in, and complains -- 'Lo, these many years do I serve thee ... and yet thou never gavest me a kid, that I might make merry with my friends: but as soon as this thy son was come, which hath devoured thy living with harlots, thou hast killed for him the fatted calf' (Luke 15:29-30). The father goes out to him and says the line the parable turns on: 'thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine. It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was DEAD, and is alive again' (Luke 15:31-32). Further rungs: the parable is the third in a set of THREE in Luke 15 about lost things being found -- the Lost Sheep, the Lost Coin, and the Lost Son.
source: PRIMARY: Gospel of Luke 15:11-32 (KJV). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Parable of the Prodigal Son' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- the request for early inheritance, the pig-feeding as the ritual-low, husks (carob pods), the father running (breaking cultural decorum), best robe / ring / sandals as tokens of restored sonship, fatted calf, elder brother's complaint, the story's placement as the third in Luke 15's lost-and-found trilogy. Rembrandt's 'Return of the Prodigal Son' (Hermitage, c. 1668) as its final visual echo. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV wording; the ring specifically as a signet ring (marker of household authority) -- flag as tradition, do not seed as a rung.
framing_note: Peak PARABLE ladder for this bank -- the CULTURAL WEIGHT is enormous; keep the scene and the named tokens (ring, sandals, robe, calf) front and centre. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (an old man RUNNING down a road, and interrupting his own son's apology to shout for a party). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: do not let a stem say 'the father forgave the son' and then ask what he did; describe the SCENE (running man, unfinished apology, servants sprinting for a ring) and the answer is the CALF, the RING, the SANDALS, or the elder brother's line. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told as the SCENE, not the theology of grace; the same voice one would use for Odysseus's return to Ithaca after twenty years or for a Celtic homecoming poem. Do NOT gloss with 'forgiveness of sins' or salvation language. DISTRACTOR MINE: the other two Luke 15 parables (Lost Sheep, Lost Coin), other 'younger vs older brother' pairs (Jacob and Esau, Cain and Abel, Joseph and his brothers), other biblical feasts (the wedding at Cana, the great supper parable). ANTI-STOCK-DETAIL: the phrase 'prodigal' just means WASTEFULLY EXTRAVAGANT -- teach that before testing it, per §16.

name: The Lost Sheep and the Lost Coin
scope: Two paired little parables that lead into the Prodigal Son. T1 (LOST SHEEP): 'What man of you, having an HUNDRED SHEEP, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it?' (Luke 15:4). T2: when he finds it, 'he layeth it on his shoulders, rejoicing' -- carrying it back like a farmer with a live lamb across his neck (Luke 15:5); a scene painted since the earliest Christian art (the 'Good Shepherd' catacomb frescoes). T3: home again, he calls his friends and neighbours and says, 'Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost' (Luke 15:6). T4 (LOST COIN): 'either what woman having TEN PIECES OF SILVER, if she lose one piece, doth not light a CANDLE, and SWEEP the house, and seek diligently till she find it?' (Luke 15:8). The coin was a drachma -- possibly one of ten strung on her headdress, the ancient equivalent of a wedding necklace. T5: when she finds it she calls her friends and neighbours together and uses almost the same words -- 'Rejoice with me; for I have found the piece which I had lost' (Luke 15:9). The two little scenes -- a shepherd on a hillside, a woman by candlelight sweeping a floor -- are told back to back, one after the other, and then Jesus goes straight into the Prodigal Son. Further rungs: the ratio-of-loss is deliberate -- 1 in 100 (sheep), 1 in 10 (coin), 1 in 2 (the Prodigal, of two sons); the sequence tightens until the loss becomes intimate.
source: PRIMARY: Gospel of Luke 15:1-10 (KJV); Matthew 18:12-14 (Matthew's version of the Lost Sheep, phrased slightly differently). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Parable of the Lost Sheep' and 'Parable of the Lost Coin' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- 99+1 ratio, shepherd carrying sheep on shoulders (Luke unique, and the primary origin of the Good Shepherd icon), Matthew's version omits the shoulder detail; ten drachmas, candle and sweeping, ancient headdress-coin tradition (a semi-scholarly speculation, not certain), the three-parable Luke 15 arc culminating in the Prodigal. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV wording; the coin-as-headdress-decoration tradition is a common devotional guess -- do NOT seed it as gospel fact.
framing_note: A compact TWIN-parable ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the shepherd carrying the sheep on his shoulders -- the original 'Good Shepherd' image, sculpted in Roman catacombs 200 years before Constantine) and T4 (a woman sweeping her floor by candlelight for one lost coin). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: describe the SCENE (a hillside with 99 sheep, a swept house, a candle) and ask for the NUMBER, the OBJECT, or the ACTION. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told as domestic scenes, not as doctrinal illustrations; the same voice as a Celtic hearth-story or an Aesop fable. DISTRACTOR MINE: other biblical shepherds (David protecting the flock from lion and bear, the shepherds at Bethlehem, Ezekiel 34 on the shepherds of Israel), other 'candle in the house' images (the lamp under a bushel, the wise virgins with their lamps). ANTI-STOCK-DETAIL: the drachma is a Greek silver coin worth about a day's wages -- teach that once, per §16.

name: The Sower and the Mustard Seed
scope: Two kingdom parables about SEEDS. T1 (SOWER): 'Behold, a sower went forth to sow' (Matthew 13:3). Jesus describes FOUR kinds of ground the seed falls on. T2: the FOUR grounds -- (1) by the WAYSIDE, where the BIRDS eat it up; (2) on STONY places, where it springs up quickly but scorches in the sun 'because it had no root'; (3) among THORNS, which grow up and choke it; (4) on GOOD ground, where it 'brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold' (Matthew 13:4-8). T3: Jesus takes his disciples aside afterward and explicitly EXPLAINS the parable (unusually -- most parables are not decoded) -- the seed is the word; the wayside is those who hear and forget; the stony ground is those who receive joyfully but fall away in trouble; the thorns are those choked by 'the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches'; the good ground is those who hear and understand and bear fruit (Matthew 13:18-23). T4 (MUSTARD SEED): 'The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of MUSTARD SEED ... which indeed is the LEAST of all seeds: but when it is grown, it is the GREATEST among herbs, and becometh a tree, so that the BIRDS of the air come and lodge in the branches thereof' (Matthew 13:31-32). T5: the black mustard plant (Brassica nigra) of Palestine really does produce a startlingly small seed (about 1 mm across) and can grow into a woody bush 10 feet tall in a single season -- Jesus is describing a real Galilean weed, not an abstraction. The pairing is Jesus's own -- both parables sit side by side in Matthew 13. Further rungs: a THIRD seed-parable in Mark -- 'the earth bringeth forth fruit of herself; first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear' (Mark 4:26-29), the only parable unique to Mark.
source: PRIMARY: Matthew 13:1-32, Mark 4:1-32, Luke 8:4-15 (KJV). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Parable of the Sower' and 'Parable of the Mustard Seed' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- four soils, Jesus's explicit exposition (rare), 30/60/100-fold yield ratios, mustard seed as one of the smallest cultivated seeds in the region, Brassica nigra as the likely species (some scholars argue Sinapis alba), the plant reaching several metres in a season, birds nesting in it as an echo of Ezekiel 17:23 and Daniel 4. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV wording.
framing_note: A twin AGRICULTURAL-parable ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (this is the one parable Jesus decodes rung-by-rung on the record) and T5 (a real 1-millimetre weed that grows into a 10-foot bush). ACCURACY RAIL: the mustard 'tree' is horticultural rhetoric -- the plant is a large HERBACEOUS bush, not an oak; do not present it as literally the largest tree. Second rail: the numbers 30/60/100 are the KJV order -- Matthew and Mark differ slightly on order (Matthew descending, Mark ascending); if a rung tests order, key Matthew. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told as farmer scenes, the same voice one would use for Hesiod's Works and Days or a Celtic seasonal poem. Do NOT gloss theologically. DISTRACTOR MINE: other seed parables (the wheat and the tares in Matthew 13, the seed growing secretly in Mark 4), other 'smallest to greatest' pairs (David vs Goliath, the widow's mite). ANTI-STOCK-DETAIL: 'kingdom of heaven' is Matthew's characteristic phrase; Mark and Luke use 'kingdom of God'; keep the wording accurate to source when quoted.

name: The Talents and the Ten Virgins
scope: Two Matthew-25 readiness parables. T1 (TALENTS): a man going on a journey calls three servants and gives them money to look after -- FIVE talents to one, TWO to another, ONE to the third, 'according to his several ability' (Matthew 25:15). A talent was an enormous unit of weight -- about 75 pounds of silver, several years' wages -- so this is a fortune. T2: the first two servants trade with their talents and DOUBLE the money; the third is afraid, digs a hole in the ground, and BURIES his talent. T3: the master returns and settles accounts. To each of the first two he says, 'Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord' (Matthew 25:21). The third confesses that he buried the money because he was AFRAID of the master; the master calls him 'wicked and slothful' and orders the buried talent taken from him and given to the man who now has ten (Matthew 25:26-28). T4 (TEN VIRGINS): 'Then shall the kingdom of heaven be likened unto ten virgins, which took their lamps, and went forth to meet the bridegroom' (Matthew 25:1). FIVE were WISE and took extra OIL in vessels with their lamps; FIVE were FOOLISH and did not. T5: the bridegroom is delayed; at midnight the cry goes up, 'Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him'. The foolish virgins' lamps are going out. They beg the wise for oil; the wise refuse, telling them to go buy their own; while they are gone, the bridegroom arrives, the door is shut, and the foolish come back to find themselves locked out -- 'I know you not' (Matthew 25:12). Further rungs: 'talent' as a word for a natural ability comes into English from THIS parable, via medieval preaching -- one of the few English words the New Testament created outright.
source: PRIMARY: Matthew 25:1-30 (KJV); Luke 19:11-27 (a related but distinct parable of the pounds/minas -- separate story, do not conflate). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Parable of the Talents' and 'Parable of the Ten Virgins' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- talent as ~75 lb weight (Attic talent), 5/2/1 distribution, burying the money as a shameful loss of nerve; ten virgins with lamps and oil, wise/foolish split, midnight cry, locked door, 'I know you not'; 'talent' entering English usage in the sense of natural ability through medieval sermons on this parable, first attested in Middle English (a widely accepted etymology). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV wording; the Attic vs Roman talent weight (Attic ~26 kg, Roman ~32 kg) -- either way, an enormous sum.
framing_note: Twin PARABLE ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (the servant who BURIED the money was the one who got scolded) and T5 (the foolish virgins actually LOCKED OUT of the wedding at midnight because they ran out of oil). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: scene = a rich man's departure, three servants, buried money / lamps at midnight, a shut door; answer = the numbers (5/2/1, 10, 5/5), the buried talent, the oil, the exact quoted line. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told as scenes, not as end-times doctrine; no eschatological gloss. DISTRACTOR MINE: the related but different Lucan parable of the pounds (ten servants, ten pounds, distinct plot); other wedding-feast parables (Matthew 22, Luke 14); other 'faithful servant' parables (Matthew 24:45-51). ANTI-STOCK-DETAIL: 'talent' as MONEY is the OLDER sense, 'talent' as ABILITY the derived one -- teach the etymology before testing it, per §16.

name: Lazarus and Dives, and the sheep and the goats
scope: Two afterlife-image parables. T1 (LAZARUS AND DIVES): a RICH MAN clothed in 'purple and fine linen' feasts sumptuously every day; a POOR beggar named LAZARUS lies at his gate, covered in sores, hoping for crumbs, with only the DOGS licking his sores (Luke 16:19-21). The rich man has no name in the gospel -- the medieval name 'Dives' is simply Latin for 'rich man'. T2: both die. Lazarus is carried by ANGELS to 'Abraham's bosom'; the rich man is in HELL, in torment (Luke 16:22-23). T3: the rich man looks up, sees Abraham 'afar off, and Lazarus in his bosom', and calls out for Lazarus to be sent to him to 'DIP THE TIP OF HIS FINGER in water, and cool my tongue; for I am tormented in this flame' (Luke 16:24). Abraham refuses -- 'between us and you there is a great gulf fixed' (Luke 16:26). T3b: the rich man begs Abraham to send Lazarus to warn his five brothers still alive; Abraham says they have Moses and the prophets. The rich man protests, 'if one went unto them from the dead, they will repent'. Abraham's reply: 'If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead' (Luke 16:31). T4 (SHEEP AND GOATS): 'When the Son of man shall come in his glory ... he shall separate them one from another, as a shepherd divideth his SHEEP from the GOATS' (Matthew 25:31-32). T5: to the SHEEP on his right he says 'come, ye blessed of my Father', because -- 'I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a STRANGER, and ye took me in: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was SICK, and ye visited me: I was in PRISON, and ye came unto me' (Matthew 25:34-36). The sheep are baffled -- when did we ever do these things to you? -- and the answer is the line: 'Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the LEAST of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me' (Matthew 25:40). The goats get the opposite verdict for the opposite reasons. Further rungs: 'Dives' as the rich man's traditional name; the six criteria of the sheep-and-goats scene became the Christian tradition's 'Seven Corporal Works of Mercy' (adding 'burying the dead' from Tobit 1:17) that inspired hospitals, hospices, and prison-visiting orders for centuries.
source: PRIMARY: Luke 16:19-31, Matthew 25:31-46 (KJV). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Rich man and Lazarus' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- the rich man's traditional Latin name 'Dives' (from Vulgate 'homo quidam erat dives'), Abraham's bosom, the great gulf, the request about the five brothers, the closing line about not being persuaded even by one risen from the dead. Grokipedia 'Sheep and Goats' -- Matthew 25's judgment scene, the six criteria, its historical influence on the corporal works of mercy tradition. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV wording; note that this 'Lazarus' is a DIFFERENT Lazarus from the brother of Martha and Mary raised in John 11.
framing_note: TWIN afterlife-parable ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (the rich man in flames asking a poor beggar to dip his FINGERTIP in water) and T5 (the sheep are given the kingdom for feeding, clothing, visiting THE STRANGER -- and did not know they were doing it to Jesus). ACCURACY RAIL: this Lazarus is the PARABLE-Lazarus, NOT the historical Lazarus of Bethany raised in John 11 -- do not conflate. Second rail: 'Dives' is not IN the gospel text -- it is a LATIN word for 'rich man' picked up as a name; teach that before testing. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told as underworld-scenes with the same voice one would give the descent of Aeneas or the Norse Hel -- 'the place of torment', 'Abraham's bosom' as a resting-place; do not doctrinally gloss with 'heaven' and 'hell' as end-state theology. DISTRACTOR MINE: the OTHER Lazarus (Bethany), other underworld scenes (Orpheus, Aeneas, Odysseus in Hades, Odin at Mimir's well), other 'rich-man-poor-man' pairings (the widow's mite, the rich young ruler). ANTI-STOCK-DETAIL: 'Abraham's bosom' is not a doctrine -- it is a Second-Temple image for the righteous dead, told as story; keep it there.
history_overlap: PHILOSOPHY owns the theodicy/justice arguments -- here it stays SCENE (rich man begging for a drop of water), not moral seminar.

name: The Sermon on the Mount and the Beatitudes
scope: The longest single teaching in the gospels, and its opening lines. T1: 'And seeing the multitudes, he went up into a mountain: and when he was set, his disciples came unto him' (Matthew 5:1) -- Jesus sits down on a HILLSIDE above the Sea of Galilee to teach, in the position of a rabbi (a rabbi taught SITTING). T2: he opens with the BEATITUDES ('blessed' statements) -- eight or nine short lines, all beginning the same way: 'BLESSED are ...'. The FIRST is 'Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven' (Matthew 5:3). T3: the most quoted lines in the middle -- 'Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth' (Matthew 5:5); 'Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy' (Matthew 5:7); 'Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God' (Matthew 5:9). T4: the sermon runs on for THREE WHOLE CHAPTERS (Matthew 5-7). It contains -- 'ye are the salt of the earth' and 'ye are the light of the world, a CITY that is set on an HILL cannot be hid' (Matthew 5:13-14); the Lord's Prayer 'Our Father which art in heaven' (Matthew 6:9-13); 'consider the LILIES of the field, how they grow ... even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these' (Matthew 6:28-29); 'ye cannot serve God and MAMMON' (Matthew 6:24); the GOLDEN RULE, 'all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them' (Matthew 7:12). T5: it ends with the parable of the TWO HOUSES -- the man who builds his house on the ROCK, and the flood cannot move it, and the man who builds on the SAND, and 'great was the fall of it' (Matthew 7:24-27). And the crowd is astonished, 'for he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes' (Matthew 7:29). Further rungs: Luke has a parallel version delivered on a LEVEL PLACE (Luke 6:17), often called the Sermon on the Plain, which is shorter and includes matching WOES to balance the blessings; the traditional site above the Sea of Galilee is now marked by the Church of the Beatitudes, an octagonal chapel built in 1938.
source: PRIMARY: Gospel of Matthew 5-7 (KJV); Luke 6:17-49 (Sermon on the Plain). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Sermon on the Mount' and 'Beatitudes' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- Matthean setting on a mountain vs Lucan plain, eight (or nine) Matthean beatitudes vs four Lucan blessings with matching woes, Lord's Prayer's placement in Matthew 6, salt-and-light metaphors, lilies of the field, Golden Rule, wise-and-foolish-builders closing, Church of the Beatitudes' 1938 Barluzzi design on Mount Eremos above Tabgha. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV wording of the specific Beatitudes and cited lines.
framing_note: A LARGE ladder for a large teaching -- has to sample the wonder-lines rather than exhaust the sermon. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (three CHAPTERS solid of teaching, from a rabbi sitting on a hillside, containing the Lord's Prayer + the Golden Rule + the salt-and-light line + the lilies-of-the-field line all in one continuous session). ACCURACY RAIL: the Beatitudes are Matthew's version; Luke's are FOUR paired with FOUR WOES -- do not mash them into one nine-item list. Second rail: 'Blessed are the meek' and 'Blessed are the poor in spirit' are two DIFFERENT lines; do not conflate. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told as a teaching-scene, the same voice one would use for the Havamal in the Poetic Edda (Odin's counsel-poem) or for the sayings of the Delphic oracle -- a body of pithy lines from a named teacher, not the axioms of a religious system. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Jesus-sayings collections (the Olivet Discourse in Matthew 24, the Farewell Discourse in John 14-17), other rabbinic 'blessed is' lines from Psalm 1 or Psalm 128, and the Ten Commandments (the other famous ethical list). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never quote the beatitude in the stem and ask for its promise; give the scene (a mountain, a sitting rabbi, a hushed crowd) and ask the FIRST word ('blessed'), the LAST parable (two builders), or the specific quoted line.
history_overlap: PHILOSOPHY owns the Golden Rule's cross-cultural parallels (Confucius's negative form, Hillel's negative form) as an ethics discussion; here the Golden Rule stays as one rung, quoted, without cross-cultural comparison.

name: The Transfiguration on the mountain
scope: The strangest vision-scene in the ministry. T1: Jesus takes only PETER, JAMES and JOHN (his 'inner three') and leads them UP a high mountain, apart, by themselves (Matthew 17:1). T2: on the mountaintop he is TRANSFIGURED before them -- 'his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light' (Matthew 17:2); Mark adds that his clothes became 'shining, exceeding white as snow; so as no fuller on earth can white them' (Mark 9:3). T3: two figures appear talking with him -- MOSES and ELIJAH (Matthew 17:3), the two greatest figures of the Hebrew Bible: the giver of the Law and the greatest of the prophets, both from centuries before. T4: PETER, overwhelmed, blurts out 'Lord, it is good for us to be here: if thou wilt, let us make here three TABERNACLES; one for thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias' (Matthew 17:4) -- Mark adds the aside 'for he wist not what to say; for they were sore afraid' (Mark 9:6). T5: a BRIGHT CLOUD overshadows them and a VOICE comes out of the cloud -- 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him' (Matthew 17:5) -- the same words the voice from heaven spoke at the baptism, now with 'hear ye him' added. The disciples fall on their faces terrified; when they look up, only Jesus remains. He tells them to say nothing of the vision to anyone until after the resurrection. Further rungs: the traditional site is MOUNT TABOR in Galilee, though Mount Hermon is a competing candidate; Peter's confused 'let us make three tabernacles' echoes the Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot); the Eastern Orthodox tradition keeps the feast on 6 August with the blessing of the first grapes.
source: PRIMARY: Matthew 17:1-9, Mark 9:2-10, Luke 9:28-36, 2 Peter 1:16-18 (KJV). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Transfiguration of Jesus' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- inner-three witnesses, whiter-than-any-fuller detail from Mark, Moses and Elijah appearing, Peter's suggestion of three tabernacles, the bright cloud and voice, echo of the baptism voice; traditional Mount Tabor vs Mount Hermon location debate; 6 August feast day. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV wording.
framing_note: A compact VISION ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (his CLOTHES turned so white that 'no fuller on earth' -- no launderer -- could bleach them that bright, per Mark) and T4 (Peter, panicking, suggesting they PITCH THREE TENTS and stay). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem name the mountain-companions and then ask 'who appeared with Jesus?'; describe the SCENE (a mountaintop, three disciples, a shining figure, two visitors from the past) and the answer is Moses and Elijah, the three tabernacles, or the voice from the cloud. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell a Homeric vision-scene (Athena appearing to Odysseus in a shining form) or Odin arriving among the Aesir cloaked in light -- a wonder-scene with the same neutral awe. DISTRACTOR MINE: the two OTHER 'voice from heaven' scenes (the baptism, and John 12:28), other 'shining face' scenes (Moses's own face shining after Sinai in Exodus 34), and the three inner-circle disciples being distinct from the Twelve (Andrew, though Peter's brother, was NOT there). ANTI-STOCK-DETAIL: 'transfigured' comes from the Greek METAMORPHOTHE (μεταμορφώθη), the same root as 'metamorphosis' -- teach that etymology before testing.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Mount Tabor and Mount Hermon as places; here the mountain is the setting.

name: Palm Sunday and the whip of cords
scope: The two dramatic public scenes that begin Holy Week. T1 (PALM SUNDAY): Jesus arrives at the outskirts of Jerusalem and sends two disciples ahead to fetch a young DONKEY -- specifically 'a colt tied, whereon yet never man sat' (Mark 11:2). T2: he rides into JERUSALEM on the donkey; the crowd spreads their GARMENTS on the road, others cut down PALM BRANCHES (John 12:13) and lay them down, and shout 'HOSANNA to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord' (Matthew 21:9). T3: 'Hosanna' is a Hebrew word meaning 'Save us, please' -- originally a cry of appeal, now used as praise. The scene mirrors, deliberately, an old line from the prophet Zechariah about a king coming to the city 'lowly, and riding upon an ass' (Zechariah 9:9) -- riding a donkey, not a warhorse. T4 (CLEANSING THE TEMPLE): almost immediately Jesus goes into the TEMPLE and finds the outer court full of MONEY-CHANGERS and men selling DOVES and cattle for sacrifice. In John's telling he makes a 'SCOURGE of small cords' (John 2:15) -- a whip -- and drives them all out, overturning the money-changers' tables and pouring their coins onto the floor. T5: he shouts, 'It is written, MY HOUSE shall be called the HOUSE OF PRAYER; but ye have made it a DEN OF THIEVES' (Matthew 21:13). It is the single most physically confrontational scene in the ministry, and Mark says that the chief priests hear about it, are afraid of him because 'all the people was astonished at his doctrine', and 'sought how they might destroy him' (Mark 11:18). Further rungs: John places the Temple-cleansing at the START of Jesus's ministry (John 2); the synoptic gospels place it at the END, in Holy Week -- this is one of the classic gospel-order divergences, and the bank should state it honestly rather than pick a side. Palm Sunday is kept as the Sunday before Easter, opening Holy Week.
source: PRIMARY: Matthew 21:1-17, Mark 11:1-19, Luke 19:28-48, John 2:13-22 and 12:12-19 (KJV); Zechariah 9:9. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Triumphal entry into Jerusalem' and 'Cleansing of the Temple' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- the young unridden donkey, palm branches (John explicitly names them; Matthew and Mark just say 'branches'), garments in the road, 'Hosanna' as a Hebrew appeal, the Zechariah 9:9 echo, the whip 'of small cords' unique to John, overturned money-changers' tables, 'house of prayer' quotation from Isaiah 56:7 + 'den of thieves' from Jeremiah 7:11, John's positioning of the cleansing at the START of the ministry versus the synoptic END. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV wording.
framing_note: TWIN opening-of-Holy-Week ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (Jesus actually MAKES A WHIP OUT OF CORDS and drives merchants out of the Temple -- the single most physically dramatic action of the ministry). ACCURACY RAIL: the WHIP appears only in JOHN's version; the synoptics have Jesus overturn tables but do not mention the whip. If a rung tests source, key John. Second rail: John and the synoptics DISAGREE on when the Temple-cleansing happened -- do NOT flatten it into a single event; if the timing comes up, note the divergence. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: the Palm Sunday scene told with the same voice as Arthur's return to Camelot to lift the sword, or Cuchulainn's arrival at Emain Macha with the beast heads on his chariot -- a king-figure arriving. The whip scene told plainly, the way one would tell Thor smashing a giant's stronghold with Mjolnir. DISTRACTOR MINE: other 'entered the city' scenes (David returning with the ark), other 'overturning tables' scenes (there is no biblical parallel, this is unique), and Zechariah's line often confused with Isaiah's suffering servant. ANTI-STOCK-DETAIL: 'Hosanna' looks like a shout of praise but is originally a plea meaning 'save us, please' -- teach that once, per §16. Also flag: palm-branches specifically are John's detail.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns the Second Temple courts; here the setting is the outer Court of the Gentiles.

name: The Last Supper, the kiss, and 'let this cup pass'
scope: The night before the crucifixion -- the meal, the garden, the arrest. T1 (LAST SUPPER): Jesus and the Twelve gather in an UPPER ROOM in Jerusalem for the Passover meal. Jesus tells them, 'One of you which eateth with me shall betray me' (Mark 14:18), and they each begin to ask 'Is it I?'. T2: at the meal Jesus takes BREAD, blesses and breaks it, and gives it to them saying 'Take, eat: this is my body' (Matthew 26:26); then he takes the CUP of wine, gives thanks, gives it to them, and says 'this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins' (Matthew 26:28). T2b: John's gospel adds a scene the synoptics do not have -- during the meal, Jesus GIRDS HIMSELF with a towel, kneels down, and WASHES the disciples' FEET (John 13:4-5), including Peter's (Peter first refuses, then over-accepts). T3 (GETHSEMANE): after the meal they go out to a garden across the Kidron valley called GETHSEMANE, 'which is at the foot of the Mount of Olives'; Jesus takes Peter, James and John a stone's throw further and asks them to KEEP WATCH while he prays. T4: he prays in agony -- 'O my Father, if it be possible, let this CUP pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt' (Matthew 26:39) -- and Luke adds that his sweat 'was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground' (Luke 22:44). Coming back, he finds the three DISCIPLES ASLEEP; 'What, could ye not watch with me one hour?' (Matthew 26:40). This happens THREE times. T5 (THE KISS): Judas Iscariot arrives with a band of soldiers and Temple police carrying LANTERNS AND TORCHES; Judas has told them in advance, 'whomsoever I shall KISS, that same is he: hold him fast' (Matthew 26:48). He walks up to Jesus and says 'Hail, master', and kisses him. Peter, in a panic, draws a SWORD and cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant, whom John names as MALCHUS (John 18:10); Jesus tells Peter to put up the sword ('they that take the sword shall perish with the sword', Matthew 26:52), and in Luke's telling touches and heals the ear (Luke 22:51). Further rungs: the Passover meal itself would have involved unleavened bread and the four ritual cups of wine; Leonardo da Vinci's 'Last Supper' (1495-98) is on a refectory wall in Milan and freezes the moment Jesus says 'one of you shall betray me'; the traditional garden of Gethsemane still holds olive trees whose root systems carbon-date to over 900 years old.
source: PRIMARY: Matthew 26:17-56, Mark 14:12-52, Luke 22:7-53, John 13:1-30 and 18:1-11 (KJV); 1 Corinthians 11:23-26 (Paul's earlier account of the bread-and-cup words). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Last Supper', 'Agony in the Garden', 'Kiss of Judas' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- upper room, Passover context (or timing dispute with John), body/blood words, footwashing unique to John, Gethsemane at foot of Mount of Olives, 'let this cup pass', sleeping disciples three times, Judas's prearranged kiss signal, Peter cutting off Malchus's ear (Malchus named only in John), Jesus healing the ear (only in Luke), Leonardo's Milan mural at Santa Maria delle Grazie, olive trees in the modern Garden of Gethsemane radiocarbon-dated (2012 study) to the 12th century AD for the trunks but with possibly older root systems. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV wording of 'this is my body' / 'this is my blood' / 'let this cup pass from me'; Malchus as John-only detail; Leonardo's exact scene.
framing_note: PASSION ladder 1 of 4 -- the night. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (sweating BLOOD, per Luke, and finding his closest friends ASLEEP three times over) and T5 (a KISS is the arrest signal, and one of the disciples has a SWORD and uses it). ACCURACY RAIL: the sweat-like-blood detail is LUCAN and appears in some manuscripts but not the earliest ones -- honest sourcing: attribute to Luke. Second rail: Malchus is named ONLY in John; the ear-healing is ONLY in Luke; do not blend gospel details as if a single account. Third rail: the traditional Garden of Gethsemane's olive trees are old but not 2,000 years old at the trunk -- flag the root-system dating honestly, do not seed 'these are the trees Jesus prayed under'. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told as a night-scene of dread and betrayal, the same voice one would give the last night of the Trojans before the wooden horse is opened, or the eve of Diarmuid's boar-hunt. Absolutely no 'the sacrifice was accepted' or 'the cup of the new covenant' theological framing in the bank's OWN voice -- quote what Jesus said, do not gloss what it 'means'. DISTRACTOR MINE: other biblical betrayals (Delilah, Absalom, Joab), other named Passover meals (the Exodus original), other named 'servants' at the arrest (Peter cuts the RIGHT ear, per Luke; if a stem tests which ear, key Luke), and the OTHER Judas (Judas of James, one of the Twelve). ANTI-STOCK-DETAIL: 'Gethsemane' is Aramaic 'gat-shemanim', 'oil press' -- teach that once.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns the Mount of Olives and the Garden of Gethsemane as places (and the modern olive trees); here they are settings.

name: Peter's denial and the cock crowing
scope: The gospels' most human scene. T1: after Jesus is arrested, Peter follows 'afar off' into the courtyard of the high priest's house, where the servants and officers have lit a CHARCOAL FIRE against the cold, and stands warming his hands (John 18:18). T2: earlier at the supper Jesus had warned Peter -- 'Verily I say unto thee, that this day, even in this night, before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice' (Mark 14:30). Peter had insisted, 'though I should die with thee, I will not deny thee in any wise' (Mark 14:31). T3: at the fire a servant-girl (Mark's 'one of the maids of the high priest') looks at Peter and says 'thou also wast with Jesus of Nazareth' (Mark 14:67). Peter denies it -- 'I know not, neither understand I what thou sayest'. T4: he moves away, and a SECOND person accuses him. He denies again. A THIRD challenges him, saying his GALILEAN ACCENT gives him away -- 'thy speech agreeth thereto' (Mark 14:70); Matthew's version has 'thy speech bewrayeth thee' (Matthew 26:73). Peter starts to CURSE and to SWEAR, 'I know not the man' (Matthew 26:74). T5: and immediately the COCK CROWS. Luke's gospel adds one line that turns the scene: 'the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter' (Luke 22:61) -- Jesus, in the courtyard being interrogated, meets Peter's eyes across the yard. Peter remembers Jesus's warning, goes outside, and WEEPS BITTERLY (Matthew 26:75). Further rungs: John's gospel is careful to specify that Peter's denials happen at a CHARCOAL FIRE -- the same Greek word (anthrakia) appears TWICE in the New Testament, the second time being the fire on the beach where the risen Jesus later restores Peter (John 21:9); the parallel is deliberate.
source: PRIMARY: Matthew 26:69-75, Mark 14:66-72, Luke 22:54-62, John 18:15-27 (KJV). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Denial of Peter' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- three denials, cockcrow, the maid at the fire, the Galilean-accent detail, Luke's unique 'the Lord turned and looked upon Peter', John's anthrakia (charcoal fire) linking Peter's denial-fire to the resurrection restoration-fire on the beach. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV wording.
framing_note: A compact ladder focused entirely on one scene. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (Peter's ACCENT gives him away -- a Galilean sound in Jerusalem) and T5 (Jesus TURNS his head and meets Peter's eyes across the courtyard). ACCURACY RAIL: Mark says the cock crowed TWICE, matching Jesus's 'before the cock crow twice' warning; Matthew, Luke and John have a single crowing. This is a genuine gospel-detail difference; if a stem asks how many, source it to Mark. Second rail: 'the Lord turned and looked upon Peter' appears only in LUKE -- do not attribute it to the others. Third rail: the charcoal-fire (anthrakia) parallel between John 18 and John 21 is a specific New Testament word-play; state it as a Johannine detail if used. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told as a scene of ordinary human weakness, the same voice one would use for Roland regretting his refusal of the Olifant, or for Cuchulainn's final approach to his death-stone -- a hero's failure, told without moralising. DISTRACTOR MINE: other 'three-fold' scenes (Elijah stretching himself on the widow's son three times, the three temptations, Balaam's donkey three times), Judas's parallel betrayal, the SECOND Peter scene by the beach fire (goes in the resurrection ladder). ANTI-STOCK-DETAIL: Peter's real name in Aramaic is Cephas (Kepha) -- 'rock' -- and Peter is the Greek form (Petros); teach that once elsewhere.

name: Pilate, the crown of thorns, and 'what is truth'
scope: The Roman trial scene, ending in mockery and scourging. T1: Jesus is taken before PONTIUS PILATE, the Roman GOVERNOR of Judea. The chief priests bring the charges; Pilate asks Jesus, 'Art thou the King of the Jews?' -- to which Jesus answers, 'Thou sayest it' (Mark 15:2). T2: in John's version Pilate presses further -- 'What is truth?' (John 18:38) -- and walks out of the room before Jesus answers. Pilate announces to the crowd, 'I find in him no fault at all'. T3: it is a custom at Passover to release a prisoner. Pilate offers the crowd Jesus or a rebel named BARABBAS -- 'a robber' in John, 'made insurrection' in Mark. The crowd shouts for Barabbas (John 18:40, Matthew 27:20-21). Pilate asks, 'What shall I do then with Jesus which is called Christ?' -- and they shout 'Crucify him' (Matthew 27:22). T3b: Matthew alone has Pilate calling for water and WASHING HIS HANDS in front of the crowd, saying 'I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it' (Matthew 27:24). T4: Pilate has Jesus SCOURGED -- a Roman whipping with a leather flail set with bone and lead -- and hands him over to the soldiers. They strip him, put a SCARLET (or purple, in Mark and John) ROBE on him, plait a CROWN OF THORNS and press it onto his head, put a REED in his right hand, and kneel down mocking him 'Hail, King of the Jews', then spit on him and beat him with the reed (Matthew 27:27-30, John 19:1-3). T5: Pilate brings him out to the crowd wearing the crown and the robe and says 'BEHOLD THE MAN' -- Ecce homo in Latin (John 19:5). The crowd still shouts 'Crucify him'. Pilate finally hands him over, and John notes the exact time: 'it was the preparation of the passover, and about the sixth hour' (John 19:14). Further rungs: Pontius Pilate is one of the few New Testament figures whose historicity is confirmed outside the Bible -- a 1961 discovery at Caesarea Maritima turned up a limestone slab (the 'Pilate Stone') bearing his name and title (PRAEFECTVS IVDAEAE); Barabbas's name means 'son of the father'; the traditional site of the scourging and 'Ecce homo' scene is on the Via Dolorosa in Jerusalem.
source: PRIMARY: Matthew 27:11-31, Mark 15:1-20, Luke 23:1-25, John 18:28-19:16 (KJV). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Pontius Pilate' and 'Crown of thorns' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- Pilate as praefectus of Judea (26-36 AD), 'what is truth' in John only, Barabbas ('son of the father'), Passover-prisoner-release custom, Matthew's unique handwashing, Roman flagellum with weighted tips, purple/scarlet robe (mocking the imperial toga), plaited crown of thorns, reed as mock sceptre, 'Ecce Homo'/'Behold the man', the 1961 Pilate Stone at Caesarea Maritima confirming his historical office. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV wording; the Pilate Stone reconstruction as PRAEFECTVS IVDAEAE (not procurator).
framing_note: PASSION ladder 2 of 4 -- the trial. Dinner-test payoff: T2 ('WHAT IS TRUTH?' asked by a Roman governor and then walked out on before an answer -- a scene philosophers have chewed on for 2,000 years) and T4 (the CROWN plaited FROM ACTUAL THORNS). ACCURACY RAIL: 'What is truth' is JOHN only. The handwashing is MATTHEW only. Do not blend. Second rail: the Pilate Stone is genuine and confirms Pilate held REAL Roman office; state that when it comes up, and use 'praefectus' (Latin) not 'procurator' (later Roman title). Third rail: this is a hard scene for kids -- the scourging is stated as a Roman punishment (bone- and lead-weighted flail), one clause, no lingering; the mockery is described (robe, crown, reed, spitting) but the beating is not visualised in gore. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: the trial scene told with the same voice as Socrates before the Athenian jury or Cuchulainn before Medb -- an accused figure facing a court, told as history-of-a-legal-scene. Do NOT use 'the Innocent' or 'the Lamb' or 'the Suffering Servant' -- name Jesus plainly. DISTRACTOR MINE: other named Roman governors in the New Testament (Felix, Festus, Gallio, Sergius Paulus), other 'crown' scenes (the crown of David, the crown of Solomon), other 'what is truth' philosophical questions (Pilate's line is the anchor). ANTI-STOCK-DETAIL: 'Ecce homo' is Latin, appearing in the Vulgate translation of John 19:5 -- teach that before testing it.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns Pontius Pilate as a Roman prefect (Josephus, Tacitus, the Pilate Stone) and the mechanics of Roman provincial administration; here the trial is the STORY-scene, and the Pilate Stone is a single 'yes he was real' rung, not a career survey.

name: Simon of Cyrene, the seven last words, and the torn veil
scope: The crucifixion itself, told scene-by-scene from the road to the tomb. T1 (SIMON OF CYRENE): Jesus is made to carry his own cross toward the execution ground. On the way, exhausted, he falls; the soldiers grab a passer-by from the crowd and MAKE HIM carry it -- 'Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus' (Mark 15:21). Cyrene is on the coast of what is now Libya; a random North African bystander is thus 'compelled to bear his cross'. T2 (GOLGOTHA): they come to a place outside the city called GOLGOTHA -- Aramaic 'the place of a skull', GOLGOTHA in Aramaic, CALVARIA in Latin (Calvary in English). Jesus is crucified between TWO THIEVES; Pilate has ordered a sign nailed above his head reading 'JESUS OF NAZARETH THE KING OF THE JEWS' in three languages -- Hebrew, Greek and Latin (John 19:19-20). T3 (THE SEVEN LAST WORDS): the gospels between them preserve SEVEN sayings from the cross -- (1) 'FATHER, FORGIVE THEM; for they know not what they do' (Luke 23:34); (2) to the thief who defended him, 'Today shalt thou be with me in paradise' (Luke 23:43); (3) to his mother and to the disciple John, 'WOMAN, BEHOLD THY SON ... behold thy mother' (John 19:26-27); (4) 'MY GOD, MY GOD, WHY HAST THOU FORSAKEN ME' (Matthew 27:46, Mark 15:34) -- in Aramaic 'Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani', the opening line of Psalm 22; (5) 'I THIRST' (John 19:28); (6) 'IT IS FINISHED' (John 19:30 -- one word in Greek, tetelestai); (7) 'Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit' (Luke 23:46). T4 (THE VEIL TORN): the moment Jesus dies, 'the VEIL OF THE TEMPLE was rent in twain from the top to the bottom' (Mark 15:38) -- the great embroidered curtain that separated the Holy of Holies from the rest of the sanctuary, split in half. T5 (THE CENTURION): the Roman CENTURION standing at the foot of the cross, seeing the way Jesus dies, says the line the gospels preserve -- 'TRULY THIS MAN WAS THE SON OF GOD' (Mark 15:39). A Roman officer, one of the executioners, is the first person in Mark's gospel to say it. Further rungs: Simon's sons Alexander and Rufus are named by Mark presumably because they were known to Mark's original audience -- Paul greets a 'Rufus, chosen in the Lord' at Romans 16:13 (possibly the same); the three languages on Pilate's sign (Hebrew, Greek, Latin) are the origin of the INRI abbreviation seen on Christian crucifixes (Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum).
source: PRIMARY: Matthew 27:32-56, Mark 15:21-41, Luke 23:26-49, John 19:16-37 (KJV). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Simon of Cyrene', 'Sayings of Jesus on the cross', 'Veil of the Temple' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- Simon named with sons Alexander and Rufus (Mark), Cyrene in modern Libya, Golgotha/Calvary, trilingual titulus with the INRI abbreviation, the two thieves (Luke's exchange with one of them), the seven distinct sayings distributed across the four gospels (Matthew/Mark share the Eloi cry, Luke has 1-2-7, John has 3-5-6), the veil-tearing at death (Mark and Matthew), Roman centurion's confession, INRI derivation. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV wording of each of the seven sayings; the Aramaic 'Eloi Eloi lama sabachthani' as recorded in Mark 15:34.
framing_note: PASSION ladder 3 of 4 -- the crucifixion. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (the Roman OFFICER in charge of the execution says the line first) and T4 (a temple curtain torn top-to-bottom at the moment of death). ACCURACY RAIL: the SEVEN sayings are drawn from FOUR different gospels -- no single gospel has all seven, and Matthew/Mark have only the 'my God, my God' cry. Attribute each saying to its source when tested. Second rail: 'Eloi Eloi lama sabachthani' is quoting Psalm 22:1 -- the opening line of a psalm; state the Psalm reference honestly rather than let the cry sound like invention. Third rail: this is the darkest scene in the ministry; state each fact plainly, do not visualise Roman crucifixion mechanics beyond the sign and the sayings. Fourth rail: the two thieves are called 'malefactors' in Luke and 'thieves' in Matthew/Mark; use 'the two thieves' as the traditional English label. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same voice one would give the death of Cuchulainn tied standing to the stone, or Balder pierced by the mistletoe dart at the assembly of the gods -- a hero's death-scene, told with weight but without doctrinal gloss. Absolutely do NOT use 'atoning sacrifice', 'died for our sins', 'the Passion' as anything other than the section-label, or 'the Lamb of God' in the bank's own voice. Quote what the sayings say, do not gloss what they 'mean'. DISTRACTOR MINE: the other named foreigners at the cross (the centurion is unnamed in the gospels; medieval tradition names him Longinus, distinct from the Longinus who traditionally pierced the side), other 'torn garments' scenes, and other Psalm quotations from the cross. ANTI-STOCK-DETAIL: 'INRI' is the Latin abbreviation for the title on the sign -- teach that before testing.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Golgotha/Calvary as a place and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre as a building; HISTORY owns Roman crucifixion as a legal-military practice. Keep this ladder inside the STORY.

name: Joseph of Arimathea and the empty tomb
scope: The burial and the discovery on Sunday morning. T1 (BURIAL): a wealthy man named JOSEPH OF ARIMATHEA -- Mark calls him 'an honourable counsellor' (a member of the Sanhedrin who had not agreed to the death sentence) -- goes to Pilate and asks for Jesus's body (Mark 15:43). Pilate, surprised he is already dead, releases the body to him. T2: Joseph takes the body down, wraps it in a LINEN cloth, and lays it in a NEW TOMB 'hewn out of the rock' -- his own tomb, which had never been used (Matthew 27:60). He rolls 'a great stone to the door of the sepulchre' (Matthew 27:60). Nicodemus, in John's account, brings 'a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about an hundred pound weight' (John 19:39). T3 (SUNDAY MORNING): early on the first day of the week, before dawn, women -- Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome, according to Mark -- come to the tomb with SPICES to properly anoint the body, worrying on the way about who will roll away the stone (Mark 16:1-3). T4: they arrive to find the STONE ALREADY ROLLED AWAY, and the tomb EMPTY. An angel (or two, in Luke and John) is there -- Matthew has one 'sitting upon' the rolled-back stone with a face 'like lightning' and 'raiment white as snow' (Matthew 28:2-3). T5: the angel's LINE -- 'He is not here: for he is risen, as he said' (Matthew 28:6), and Luke's more famous version, 'WHY SEEK YE THE LIVING AMONG THE DEAD? He is not here, but is risen' (Luke 24:5-6). The women are told to go tell the disciples. Further rungs: Mary Magdalene, in John's version, stays weeping at the tomb after the others have left; she sees a man she takes to be the gardener, who says her name, 'MARY', and she recognises him -- 'Rabboni', teacher (John 20:14-16); Jesus tells her not to hold him but to go tell the others. In some medieval legends (Glastonbury, Britain) Joseph of Arimathea travels to Britain and plants his staff, which grows into the Glastonbury thorn -- a folk-tradition legend, not gospel.
source: PRIMARY: Matthew 27:57-28:10, Mark 15:42-16:8, Luke 23:50-24:12, John 19:38-20:18 (KJV). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Joseph of Arimathea', 'Empty tomb', 'Resurrection of Jesus' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- Joseph as a Sanhedrin member who dissented, the linen cloth, the new rock-cut tomb, the great stone, Nicodemus's 100 pounds of myrrh and aloes, the women's names (Mark's list differs slightly from Matthew/Luke), the angel(s), 'why seek ye the living among the dead' unique to Luke, Mary Magdalene's garden recognition unique to John (the 'noli me tangere' scene), and the medieval Glastonbury legend of Joseph in Britain (which the bank flags as legend, not gospel). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV wording; note Mark's original ending at 16:8 with the women fleeing in fear (the longer ending 16:9-20 being a later addition).
framing_note: PASSION ladder 4 of 4 -- burial and Sunday morning. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (a hundred pounds of MYRRH AND ALOES, per John, an emperor's-funeral scale of spice for a private burial) and T5 (an angel saying 'why are you looking for THE LIVING among THE DEAD' in Luke's version). ACCURACY RAIL: the four gospels differ on the details of the empty tomb -- number of women, number of angels, exactly what is said. Do NOT blend them; if a rung tests a detail, key the source gospel. Second rail: the Glastonbury Joseph legend is MEDIEVAL and traditional -- do NOT seed it as a gospel fact; the bank may include one 'further rungs' mention of the legend as legend. Third rail: the 'Rabboni' scene in the garden is JOHN-only; if a rung uses Mary Magdalene mistaking Jesus for the gardener, source it to John. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told as a story of grief and discovery, the same voice one would give the return of Persephone or the recovery of Balder's ship-funeral -- solemn wonder, not doctrinal proof. Do NOT gloss with 'proof of the resurrection'; state what the women found, and what the angel said. DISTRACTOR MINE: the other Marys (mother of Jesus, of Bethany, of Clopas), other 'rolled stone' scenes (the stone rolled from the well for Rachel in Genesis 29), other named tomb-owners, and the confusion between the two Josephs (father Joseph vs Joseph of Arimathea). ANTI-STOCK-DETAIL: 'Rabboni' is Aramaic for 'my teacher/master' -- teach that once.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the traditional Garden Tomb site; HISTORY owns Roman burial practice. Keep this ladder inside the story.

name: Emmaus, Doubting Thomas, and the 153 fish
scope: The three great post-resurrection encounter scenes. T1 (EMMAUS): on the same Sunday afternoon, two disciples are walking from Jerusalem to a village called EMMAUS, about seven miles away, talking sadly over the last few days. A STRANGER falls in beside them and asks what they are discussing (Luke 24:13-19). T2: they explain everything -- 'we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel' -- and the stranger, walking with them, opens the Scriptures to them, 'beginning at Moses and all the prophets ... the things concerning himself' (Luke 24:27); they do not recognise him because 'their eyes were holden' (Luke 24:16). T3: they reach the village and invite him to stay for the evening meal. When the stranger sits down, TAKES BREAD, BLESSES IT, BREAKS IT and gives it to them -- 'THEIR EYES WERE OPENED, and they knew him; and he vanished out of their sight' (Luke 24:30-31). They say to each other 'Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?' (Luke 24:32). T4 (DOUBTING THOMAS): that same Sunday evening the disciples are gathered behind LOCKED DOORS 'for fear of the Jews', and Jesus appears among them and says 'Peace be unto you' (John 20:19). THOMAS is not there. When they tell him, he says: 'Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe' (John 20:25). T4b: eight days later Jesus appears again, doors still shut, and turns straight to Thomas: 'Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing' (John 20:27). Thomas answers 'MY LORD AND MY GOD' (John 20:28). T5 (THE 153 FISH AND PETER'S RESTORATION): back in Galilee, Peter and six of the disciples fish all night on the Sea of Galilee and catch nothing. At dawn a figure on the shore tells them to cast the net on the right side of the boat; they do, and it fills to bursting. John (the beloved disciple) says to Peter, 'It is the Lord', and Peter jumps into the water and swims for shore. Jesus is standing at a CHARCOAL FIRE cooking BREAD and FISH (John 21:9). They haul the net to shore -- 'and yet was not the net broken' -- and count the catch: exactly ONE HUNDRED AND FIFTY-THREE (John 21:11). Then, at the fire, Jesus asks Peter THREE TIMES 'Simon, son of Jonas, LOVEST THOU ME?' -- once for each of Peter's three denials at the earlier charcoal fire; Peter is grieved by the third asking, and answers each time 'thou knowest that I love thee', and each time Jesus tells him 'Feed my sheep' (John 21:15-17). Further rungs: the ANGLE 153 has been discussed for two millennia -- Jerome (4th century) claimed there were 153 known species of fish; St Augustine offered a triangular-number reading (1+2+3+...+17=153); no clear meaning has been settled and the honest position is that we simply do not know why John records the exact number.
source: PRIMARY: Luke 24:13-35 (Emmaus), John 20:19-29 (Thomas), John 21 (the 153 fish and Peter). KJV. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Road to Emmaus appearance', 'Doubting Thomas', 'Miraculous catch of fish' (browser, 2026-09-04) -- Emmaus at ~7 miles from Jerusalem (or ~60 stadia in Luke, actual village disputed), unrecognised until the breaking of bread, 'their eyes were opened', Thomas absent then present, invitation to touch the wounds, 'My Lord and my God', post-resurrection Galilean fishing scene, the exact 153 fish, charcoal fire echoing Peter's denial fire (both scenes use anthrakia in John), three-fold 'do you love me' matching three denials, Jerome's fish-species reading, Augustine's triangular-number reading, no scholarly consensus on the number's meaning. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: KJV wording of Thomas's 'my Lord and my God' and Peter's 'thou knowest that I love thee'.
framing_note: The RESURRECTION-encounter ladder that closes the whole life. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (they recognise him ONLY when he breaks the bread, and then he vanishes) and T5 (the specific count of ONE HUNDRED AND FIFTY-THREE fish, and the three-times-repeated 'do you love me' one for each denial). ACCURACY RAIL: Emmaus's actual location is disputed; state the ~7-mile distance from Jerusalem and do not commit to a specific modern site. Second rail: Thomas's 'my Lord and my God' is his line in the SCENE -- do NOT invoke it as a doctrinal proof-text; it is what a startled man said when he saw someone he thought was dead. Third rail: the 153 fish has NO agreed meaning; the bank presents Jerome's and Augustine's readings honestly as ancient GUESSES, never as 'the answer'. Fourth rail: the charcoal-fire link between John 18 (denial) and John 21 (restoration) uses the same Greek word twice in the New Testament (anthrakia) -- key that as a Johannine detail. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told as scenes of recognition and reconciliation, the same voice one would use for Odysseus revealed to Penelope by the bed's secret or by his old dog Argos, or for Fionn's father returning in vision. Do NOT use 'the risen Lord' or 'the glorified Christ' as the bank's own language; call him 'Jesus' or 'the stranger' as the scenes themselves do. DISTRACTOR MINE: other named post-resurrection encounters (Paul on the Damascus road -- that belongs to a separate Paul ladder, not here), the other 'do you love me' pairs (Ruth and Naomi, Jonathan and David), other named fish-catches (Jonah's fish, the fish with the coin in its mouth in Matthew 17). ANTI-STOCK-DETAIL: 'Doubting Thomas' is the traditional English nickname for the apostle called Didymus (John 20:24) -- 'Didymus' means 'twin'; teach that before testing.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Emmaus as a place (disputed sites: al-Qubeibeh, Amwas/Nicopolis, Motza, Abu Ghosh) and the Sea of Galilee shore. HISTORY does not own these scenes.
